events.title: Research open-source avatar bases
events.input:

Goal: I'm building a browser-based real-time voice AI companion with a 3D anime avatar (VTuber-style: lip sync, blinking, idle motion, emotional expressions, reacts while talking), similar in genre to the animated voice companions in the Grok app. It will be a web app on free hosting (Vercel or Render free tier — so NO GPU server and no long-running heavy backend; rendering must happen in the browser, AI via hosted APIs). I want to start from an existing open-source project rather than from scratch.

Find and evaluate the best open-source bases. Candidates I already know of, which you should verify the current state of (last commit date, stars, license, stack, whether it runs purely in-browser + serverless API routes): pixiv/ChatVRM, semperai/amica, moeru-ai/airi, Open-LLM-VTuber/Open-LLM-VTuber, met4citizen/TalkingHead, pixiv/three-vrm (the library), zoan37/ChatVRM forks, any Next.js forks of ChatVRM with streaming TTS. Also search GitHub and X/Twitter/Reddit for newer projects (2025-2026) specifically described as open-source clones/alternatives of Grok companions, or "AI waifu" web apps with VRM avatars and realtime voice.

- repo URL, license (flag anything non-permissive or with avatar-asset restrictions), last activity, stars
- tech stack and whether it deploys on Vercel/serverless without a persistent server
- how it does lip sync (volume-based vs viseme), expressions, blinking, idle animation (VRMA / Mixamo retarget)
- how hard it is to swap in a streaming LLM + streaming TTS provider and add barge-in/interruptions
- known problems (stale deps, broken builds, open issues)

The tracker is live under ValoqLmao, and it already shows a first working avatar build: **https://valoqlmao.github.io/project-tucker/**

## The account switch
- **New home:** repo, feed and page are all under ValoqLmao, with fresh git history authored only by that account.
- **Old copy:** I couldn't delete the repo under the first account because the `gh` token lacks the `delete_repo` scope. I made it private and removed its Pages site and feed branch, so nothing is publicly readable. The old page URL may still show a cached empty shell for a few more minutes.
- **To delete it fully:** run `! gh auth refresh -h github.com -s delete_repo -u <that account>` and tell me, or delete it in the repo's GitHub settings.
- **Scrubbing:** the old account name, your real name and your email are stripped from the public feed, including from your own message that mentioned the account.

## What the tracker shows
- **Feed:** every prompt, my replies and each tool call (commands, file names), refreshed about once a minute.
- **Not published:** tool output is never shown, and anything that looks like a credential is redacted. This is pattern-based, so don't paste real API keys into chat; put them in a `.env` file instead.
- **Live build panel:** the running app, embedded.
- **Updates:** it refreshes while this session is open and at each turn in future sessions.

## Research verdicts
- **Base:** no open-source project is a clean fork. The good ones are either stale (ChatVRM, Amica), non-commercial or AGPL (aituber-kit, Utsuwa), or a huge Vue monorepo (AIRI). I'm building a thin app directly on `three-vrm`.
- **Voice stack:** this is the lowest-latency setup that fits free hosting, at an estimated 1.1–1.5 s from end of speech to first audio and roughly $1–2 per hour of conversation.

  | Layer | Pick | Fallback |
  |---|---|---|
  | Speech-to-text | Deepgram Flux | Soniox |
  | LLM | Venice uncensored models | xAI Grok |
  | Voice | Cartesia Sonic (emotion tags) | Inworld TTS (gives mouth-shape data for lip sync) |

- **Hosting problem:** Vercel's free plan is non-commercial only, and its acceptable-use policy bans "obscene" content, which puts the NSFW persona at risk on any Vercel plan. Render's free tier has a one-minute cold start, which is too slow for this. I'll research a host for the small API piece before building it.

## First avatar build
It uses a placeholder model from the `three-vrm` examples, whose licence allows redistribution. It blinks, breathes, sways, glances away and back, cross-fades between six emotions, and moves its mouth to your mic. I checked it in Chrome: it loads without console errors and the happy expression works. I did not test the mic lip sync.

## What I need from you
1. **API keys:** sign up for Deepgram, Venice, and Cartesia (or Inworld). All have free credit; nothing can talk until these exist.
2. **The character:** make her in VRoid Studio (free) and export as VRM 1.0, so the model is yours with no licence strings. I can't produce a good original anime model myself.
3. **Old repo:** say whether you want it fully deleted (see above).

Next I'm researching the API host and then building the talk loop (mic, streamed reply, voice, interruptions) so it's ready to plug keys into.

The research on Grok and other live-character systems came back, and I've applied a second round of face improvements from it. Reload http://localhost:5173 to see them.

## What the research found about Grok
- The companions' models and animation came from an outside studio, Animation Inc., not from xAI itself.
- From a leaked (unofficial) config, Ani uses a small fixed set of emotions (curiosity, shyness with a blush, excitement, love, stress, sadness, frustration) plus a handful of canned moves such as "peek" (come closer), "tease", "spin" and "sway".
- A second AI pass watches the conversation and triggers those reactions; the dialogue model itself is told never to speak stage directions.
- What makes her feel alive is mostly reactions timed to the conversation, blushes and heart effects, moving toward the camera, and voice tone. It is not an unusually detailed face.

So the face layer I built in the last round already has more range than theirs. What we lack is their reaction moves and effects.

## What I added from it
- **Body language per expression:** each feeling now comes with a head tilt, a gaze shift or a lean. Curious tilts her head and leans in, shy drops her chin and looks away, smug lifts it.
- **Camera moves closer:** on warm, flirty or curious moments the camera eases in slightly, like Ani's "peek".
- **Staggered timing:** eyes react first, then brows, then mouth, then the head follows, which is how real faces move.
- **Blink on expression change:** people blink as their expression shifts, and it hides the switch.
- **Resting drift:** mouth corners, lids and brows drift slightly even when nothing is happening.

I have not looked at this round in the browser at all; it compiles and builds, and that is the extent of the check. If a tilt or lean looks exaggerated, tell me which mood and I'll tune it.

1. **Reaction moves:** a few short canned animations (lean in, look away shyly, hair flick, small laugh) triggered by the conversation. This is the biggest thing Grok has that we don't.
2. **Blush overlay:** a cheek blush that works on every model, since half of yours lack the built-in one.
3. **Eye sparkle:** a slight shimmer on the eye highlights, which is what makes anime eyes look wet and alive.
4. **Soft glow and background:** light bloom and a real backdrop instead of the flat dark colour.

events.text:
Grub is fixed, the backgrounds are real scenes, and everything needed to host it is built and tested locally. Here's what changed, then the deployment steps.

## What changed
- **Grub:** the cause was a line I'd put in every persona telling them to drop the act if you seemed distressed, and the model was reading trash talk as distress. It now only applies if you plainly and sincerely say you're in crisis. Grub and Vex are also told to fire back harder and never check on your feelings. I tested your exact scenario ("am I okay? no, because I'm stuck talking to you") and Grub replied "Staring at your keyboard hoping it will magically transform into a whiskey bottle, are we?"
- **Backgrounds:** three real panoramic scenes with a picker: a night city skyline (the default), a fireside room and a lounge. They're free-to-use photos from Poly Haven, so they can be hosted publicly. The last one I tested is saved in your browser, so you may see Fireside first.
- **Cloudflare server:** a Workers version of the session server. I ran it in Cloudflare's own runtime on this machine and it handled typed and spoken conversations, including two spoken turns in a row.
- **Entry screen:** an 18+ checkbox and an access code. Without the code nobody can start a session, so strangers can't spend your Fish, Deepgram and OpenRouter credit. Tested: wrong code is refused, right code gets in.

## Deployment
Two pieces go on Cloudflare: the **site** on Pages at `tucker.valoq.dev`, and the **server** as a Worker at `tucker-api.valoq.dev`. Change those names in `server\wrangler.toml` first if you want different ones.

### 1. Deploy the server
In a terminal, from the project folder:

```
cd server
npx wrangler login
npx wrangler secret put FISH_API_KEY
npx wrangler secret put DEEPGRAM_API_KEY
npx wrangler secret put OPENROUTER_API_KEY
npx wrangler secret put ACCESS_CODE
npx wrangler deploy
```

- `wrangler login` opens your browser to approve access to your Cloudflare account.
- Each `secret put` prompts you to paste a value. Use the same keys that are in your `.env`. For `ACCESS_CODE`, make up the code you'll give to people; make it long.
- `deploy` creates `tucker-api.valoq.dev` automatically, because your domain is already on Cloudflare.

### 2. Deploy the site
In the Cloudflare dashboard: **Workers & Pages → Create → Pages → Connect to Git**, and pick the `project-tucker` repo. Then set:

| Setting | Value |
|---|---|
| Root directory | `app` |
| Build command | `npm run build:pages` |
| Build output directory | `dist` |
| Environment variable | `VITE_API_URL` = `https://tucker-api.valoq.dev` |

Save and deploy. Then open the new Pages project → **Custom domains → Set up a domain** → `tucker.valoq.dev`.

### 3. Try it
Open `https://tucker.valoq.dev`, tick the 18+ box, enter your access code, and talk.

## Things to know before you share the link
- **The characters won't be there.** The hosted site shows the placeholder model. The six game characters are local-only by design, and they also can't go on Pages: each is 37–62 MB and Pages caps files at 25 MB. One of the free VRoid Hub models I linked earlier (about 20 MB) would fit. Tell me which you want and I'll wire it in as the hosted default.
- **Your prompts are public.** The repo is public, so the persona prompts and code are visible to anyone. Your keys are not; they live only in Cloudflare's secrets and your local `.env`.
- **Costs are yours.** Everyone with the code spends your credit. Sessions are capped at 45 minutes each, but there's no per-person spending limit yet.
- **What I couldn't test:** the real Cloudflare deployment. Local testing used the same runtime, but the free plan's usage limits only apply once it's live. If the server misbehaves there, the fallback from my earlier research is Fly.io, and the existing Node server runs on it unchanged.

events.text:
A security review of the deployment code raised two gaps, and I've closed both. The deployment steps I gave you are unchanged.

- **Per-person session cap:** the Cloudflare server had no limit on how many conversations one person could open at once, so someone with the code could have run many in parallel on your credit. It now allows two per connection and refuses a third. Tested locally: two open, the third is refused, and closing one frees a slot.
- **Code-guessing limit:** the limit on wrong access-code attempts could be reset by flooding it with requests from many addresses. It now only forgets attempts once they've expired, and refuses new guesses if it ever fills up.

The guess limit is still best-effort on Cloudflare, because it lives in memory and Cloudflare can run several copies of the server. So the real protection is the access code itself: make it long and random, not a word.

The local test site at http://localhost:5173 is still running as before, with no access code needed.

events.text:
The security review flagged three follow-up issues in the limits I'd just added, and all three are fixed and pushed. Nothing changes in the deployment steps.

- **Address handling:** the per-person limits identified visitors by a crude cut of their network address, which the same person could dodge by writing an IPv6 address in a different form. Addresses are now parsed properly, so short and long forms count as the same visitor.
- **Lockout risk:** my previous fix refused all new visitors if the wrong-code tracker filled up, which would have let an attacker lock everyone out of entering the code. It now drops its oldest entry to make room, and there's an overall ceiling of 300 guesses per ten minutes from everyone combined.
- **Stuck session slots:** if a connection died without closing cleanly, it could keep holding one of a visitor's two conversation slots. The slot is now also released when the 45-minute session limit fires.

I tested the address parsing and the limiter with sample cases and they behave as described. I did not re-run a full conversation through the Cloudflare version after this last change, since it only touched the limiter and one timer line.

One more security fix to the access-code limiter is pushed; the deployment steps are still unchanged.

The overall guess ceiling I added last round could be used up by a single visitor hammering wrong codes, which would have blocked everyone else from entering the code for ten minutes. In a test, one visitor making 50 attempts used only 3 of the shared budget, and other visitors still got through.

One trade-off remains and is inherent to the design: someone attacking from hundreds of different addresses can still reach the shared ceiling and briefly block code entry. That's the price of also stopping them from guessing the code that way. People who are already in are not affected, since their access lasts 12 hours.

Done and deployed. Every session folder now also contains a **`conversation.wav`**: the whole exchange in order (you, her, you, her) as one file you can just play. The individual per-turn files are still saved alongside it.

## How it works
- Each spoken turn is added to the file as it happens, with a third of a second of silence between turns.
- Your mic audio and her voice are recorded at different quality levels, so your side is converted to match hers and the file plays at one consistent speed.
- `transcript.json` now gives each turn a `conversationAt` value: the second where that turn starts in `conversation.wav`. That lets your other project jump straight to any turn.

## What it leaves out
- **Typed turns:** there's no audio for them, so they appear in the transcript only.
- **Real pauses:** the file is the turns back to back, so it doesn't preserve how long you actually waited between them. The transcript's timestamps have the real times.
- **Interrupted replies:** it includes the audio the server had generated up to the point you cut in, which can be slightly more than you actually heard.

## What I tested
- **Local server:** a two-turn spoken conversation. The combined file was 22.34 s, matching the four turns plus pauses, and each turn's start time lined up.
- **Cloudflare's runtime on this machine:** a four-turn conversation with long replies, about 4.5 minutes of audio. Large files upload in pieces there, so this was the risky path. The assembled file came back at 13 MB with the correct length and sound throughout.
- **Not tested:** the live site, since I don't have your access code. After your next conversation there, the session folder in the R2 bucket should have `conversation.wav` next to the transcript.

One limitation on the live site: the combined file is finalised when the conversation ends, meaning when you close the tab or the session times out. If the server is cut off abruptly mid-conversation, the per-turn files and transcript will still be there, but that session's `conversation.wav` will be missing.

| **Sees your screen** | Chrome's screen share (`getDisplayMedia`) grabs frames, and a screenshot goes to the model every few seconds or when someone talks. Your current models (unslopnemo etc.) are text-only, so this needs a vision model, either as the main brain or as a cheap "describe what's happening" step feeding the persona. | Easy |
| **Hears teammates** | Valorant has its own voice chat output device setting. Point it at a virtual audio cable (VB-Cable or Voicemeeter) and Tucker gets clean teammate voices without gunfire, while you still hear them through a monitor. | Medium, mostly audio routing setup |
| **Talks in VC** | Tucker's voice plays into a second virtual cable, which Valorant uses as its mic. Voicemeeter mixes your real mic in so you can still talk too. | Medium |
| **Holds V while talking** | A browser can't press keys, so a tiny local helper holds V from reply start to reply end. | Easy to write, but see the first risk |
| **Replies only when talked to** | Trigger on his name, or let the model decide each turn whether to answer or stay quiet. | Medium, needs tuning |

Things to know before building:

- **Vanguard and fake keypresses:** I can't promise Vanguard lets a simulated V through; it blocks some injected input. This is the one piece that needs testing on your machine first.
- **Ban risk:** Screen capture and audio routing are what OBS and Voicemod do, so nothing touches the game. An AI making callouts from your screen is a gray area under Riot's third-party rules, though, and a rude persona mouthing off to randoms can get *your* account comms-banned from reports.
- **Latency:** Expect about 1.5–3 seconds from a teammate finishing to Tucker speaking. That is fine for banter and reactions, but too slow for "he's behind you" callouts.
- **Who's talking:** All teammates arrive as one mixed stream, so he won't know who said what unless we read the speaker icons off the screen or add speaker separation.
- **Recording:** The app currently saves every conversation to disk. For VC mode I'd turn that off, since it would be recording strangers.

I'd build it in this order, since each step works on its own:

1. Screen vision in the existing app, so he reacts to your game while talking only to you.
2. Hearing VC through the virtual cable.
3. Talking into VC with the V-hold helper.

## How it works
1. Open **Game**. **Mode** is set to "Director: I say it, Rudi says it their way".
2. Pick the key under **Hold this key to talk to them**. It defaults to Mouse 5; other choices are Mouse 4, middle mouse, Caps Lock, Left Alt, the key under Esc, and a few letters.
3. Press **Start game mode**. No screen share is needed.
4. In game, hold the key, say what you want said, and let go. He rewrites it in the persona, holds V, and says it into voice chat.

The key works while Valorant is in front. It isn't blocked from the game, so pick one Valorant doesn't use. Pressing it again while he's still talking cuts him off and starts a new line.

## What I tested
I ran it with a simulated key hold and synthetic voice lines. He started speaking about 0.7 to 1.2 seconds after the key came up.

| You say | Rudi says |
|---|---|
| "Two of them are pushing B main, I need a smoke on heaven right now." | "Two of them are pushing B main, I need a fucking smoke on heaven right now, dipshits." |
| "Nice shot Sova, that was really clean." | "Nice shot, Sova. That was fucking clean." |
| "Does anyone have money to buy me a rifle this round?" | "Fucking hell, I'm out of cash. Somebody spot me a rifle this round, would ya?" |

- **He's told to keep every fact and only add attitude.** Praise stays praise, and callouts stay short. Each line is rewritten on its own, with no memory of earlier ones, because that's what kept him faithful.

- **Agent names are recognised now.** "Sova" was coming out as "server", so the speech-to-text is given the Valorant agent and weapon names.
- **Not tested with your real mic, a real mouse button, or Valorant itself.** I also didn't re-check the dialog in the browser after my last small fix, which makes it re-ask the server what it supports each time it opens.
